notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00457.opp-gr: In §2 the transmitted text includes the edition's list of manuscript sigla (C, A, P, I, Par), a stray marginal intrusion; it has been left untranslated. §10: 'knowing the second part and having seen the third' renders εἰδότες μὲν οἵδε τὰ δεύτερα, ἰδόντες δὲ τὰ τρίτα literally; the reference is obscure. 'Belts' (ζῶναι) denote offices held. 'The governor of the eastern cities' is presumably the comes Orientis. 'Alexander' in §12 is likely an official seated with Severus; not securely identified.

18.2: 'even if the night says otherwise' (εἰ καὶ ἡ νὺξ ἕτερα λέγει) is obscure; perhaps a proverbial phrase or a sign of corruption. 25.1: the words in angle brackets are an editorial supplement. 26: 'that Libyan, that Irus, then Midas' — the Libyan figure is unidentified; Irus (the beggar of the Odyssey) and Midas seem to be used as contemptuous nicknames, and the reference may be to a contemporary official. 22.1: 'put the governor in chains' renders δήσω literally; the sense is presumably figurative or ironic. 32.1: 'jump across to him' — sense uncertain; possibly meaning Malchus would not have defected to Severus' side.

36.2 (ch. 37): 'nor does time stand still to see this' renders ἱστᾶι as printed; the sense is that no time, even in the underworld, will bring reconciliation. 46.1: the governors' imagined words are obscure; 'knows not how great a governor is' renders οἶδεν οὐκ ὢν as printed, which may be corrupt. 44.1: the Isocrates allusion (judging the unseen from the seen) is in 43 as printed with κὰγ for κατ᾿.

48: ἴδει is read as ἔδει ('had to'). ἰνὶ is read as ἔνι. 'Mareas' and 'Victor' could not be further identified. 49: 'καὶ οἳ]' and 50 'καὶ]', 51 'ἐν]' contain stray brackets from the edition, ignored. 'Medea' (Μηδείας) may be a pun on Media; uncertain.

nodes.text: LVII.
AGAINST SEVERUS.

Those who are to judge for us are present, and they have kindly heeded [the summons] as the god was rising; and there is no need of any oath towards us that you will indeed guard what is just. For you have spent your whole life in respecting and guarding what is just, and your character would serve you in place of oaths, so that I fully expect you will judge that I do no wrong, even if Fortune is not equal between me and my opponents.

2. Now I for my part expected the good Antiochus, even if he could not accuse [Severus] for what had been done, because he lives under Severus and could easily be harmed, at least to stay silent, and in that way at least, if in no other, to pay some regard to justice. But since he both talks a great deal and finds fault, and would like me to change my mind and be where I was before, I pray that he may be won over by me, without our friendship being harmed by any of these present matters. But if he is in fact vexed at not having taken me and brought me to Severus, I shall ask him to forgive me if I imitate, in matters concerning myself, the zeal he shows on behalf of others.
3. Bear with me, gentlemen of the jury, while I speak briefly from the beginning. For you will see that I do no wrong even in what I am doing now.

This man was handed over to me by his father, who praised my generosity in the matter of fees and trusted that the one who would not pay would be on an equal footing with those who paid. But in the second year, after making some commotion at the door, he ran in, took hold of the boy, and dragged him off to contests, the courtroom and lawsuits.

Seeing this, I said: "This boy, at his age? At the very start of his training? How will he bear the face of the judge? How the boldness of the advocates? How the very appearance of the court?" Hearing this, he said that I was talking nonsense and that he would not be persuaded. Being unable to prevail over the father, I asked the gods that no harm should come from the ill-advised plan by which he was taking the young man away.

And indeed, it was not yet the third year, and there was much talk that Severus had great power as an advocate, then very great, then that all who were accustomed to win had been defeated. And there were those who said that gold had been given for him to a sorcerer, and that what was happening was the work of that man's skill, not the orator's, and that the absence of anything fine in his speeches bore witness to this.

Well then, I heard of the victories with pleasure, but of these things without pleasure; and in the second and third [years], when the same things kept happening (for he kept winning), and the same things were again being bandied about, again I was pleased by the one and vexed by the other, acting the part of a friend in both.

After this, then, when a great stream of good fortune came, more astonishing and giving greater scope to the talk about the sorcerer, I laughed at those who spoke of the sorcerer, judging that all this was due to oratory and fine character; and Severus did not fail to notice that I both rejoiced in his honours and took pride in them.

And both when going to Egypt and back from there to the emperor, he did everything by which he thought he would seem to be just towards me, and called himself a lover of my old age. And when he attained these two belts of office he now holds, he honoured me with letters and said that what would most of all bring him here was me. And many such [letters] came from Thrace, and some came also from the city of Tarsus, through the middle of which the river Cydnus flows.

He said all this, to the effect that he considered himself wronged by not having seen me and was eager to see me. And when we first met, having dismounted, with the governor of the eastern cities standing near him, he greeted me with more kisses than each of the others, and this caused no small delay.

Now those to whom he caused confusion and fear both on his arrival and as he was about to arrive, these men here knowing the second part and having seen the third, hoping that they would have one safety, one recourse and one refuge, namely Severus' respect for me, all together rushed to me and to these knees: some because they had done me some service, while for others this itself was a claim, that I had helped many without having received any kindness first. So on the same day, in the evening, when he permitted it, I went off and reported just these things: the people's hope, and their running to me, and that he had it in his power to make me a benefactor of my own fellow citizens and to make me more honoured.

11. Now Homer says: "and he entreated all the <Achaeans>, but most of all the sons of Atreus"; and I, pleading on behalf of all, did this most of all on behalf of Malchus, because the dangers were greater as a result of greater slanders.

Severus was kind in his words, and said he would honour Zeus Meilichios [the Gentle] with his mildness, so that Alexander, sitting beside him, praised his readiness for this. What then followed? He told those in chains to take heart and to tell him all the truth about everything, and Malchus, among other things, also how the gold would come to light. These matters the governor held over on the following day, but on the day after that he took them up.

And how he will deal with the others, god knows; but as for Malchus' case, it would have been better for him to die three times and become a dinner for Polyphemus than to suffer what he has suffered, while our constitution remains and has not been overthrown. For things that no one could bear without tears even if men of the marketplace suffered them, these were suffered by a man who has held office, who received a belt, a throne, the right to judge from the ruler, who has given orders to soldiers, to whom the emperor has often written.

For being no longer able to hide his hatred, nor to hold out against its magnitude, he poured out all that lay in his heart, not far short of madness. "And let him be stripped of his cloak"; and it was on the ground; "and of his first tunic"; and the tunic was on the ground; "and of the third, the linen one"; and this too was with the others.

This was dreadful too, and there was no one who was not appalled; but while most thought he would stop there, Malchus was hoisted up, laid out for the blows to come, and bundles of rods were seen on the ground. As those worn out by the blows were thrown aside each time, other fresh ones were needed. The same happened with the floggers: a fresh man took over from the one who gave up, and the last was the tenth. Of these, six spent their strength on his back, and the sides drained four upon themselves, since this man ordered the rod-bearers to take the sides instead of the back. And much was the blood that flowed, and many the pieces of flesh scattered about, cut from the body by the blows; and Malchus cried out until the middle of them, but from then on he was beaten in silence, his sufferings having taken from him even the power to cry out.

What other punishment could one have added to these? You took away the tablet by which he held office. You stripped him not of some garments and not others, but of all of them. As for the blows, no one could even count them. Leave, then, to the doctors and to his family the ravines in his body, in case they can somehow make what has gaped apart come together. But he went on to another thing, far more painful for the sufferer and more pitiable for those who saw it. He handed over to men who were to lead it through the city that fine spectacle, the depths in his body; and there was no one who did not groan and strike his face and lament for the laws undone.

The trousers too carried a certain outrage: as much of them as was above the thighs had been exposed by the rods, and they had lost their function, being unable to cover. And when Malchus asked for something of the kind that he could put before his eyes so as not to see those looking at him, there was no one who would give it, though many would gladly have given it, but were held back by fear of what they were seeing.

The same fear also deprived Malchus of thorough treatment, since some doctors did not come near him, and others did not use all the means available, knowing that he would be most pleased to hear that Malchus was dead. And that they had been reasonably convinced of this, this man himself bore witness, being so disposed at the report that went round about his death that he was even seen leaping for joy.

19. Well then, having done all these things, so contrary to my entreaties on behalf of Malchus, he says he is wronged because I do not visit him, and he has sent Antiochus to persuade me to do as before. But if you can undo what has been done, Antiochus, and make it not to have happened, let us walk, let us go, even if the night says otherwise; but if not even one of the gods could do this, why do you try to persuade one who shares in Malchus' disgrace to shame himself and to confess before everyone that he is without feeling and the sort to bow down to those who outrage him?

20. 'For I caught Malchus', he says, 'doing wrong concerning the emperor's gold.' I know that he committed some such offence, deceived by villainous men with hopes both sweet and terrible for a man to entertain. But we know that this business of deception has laid hold even of the greatest of the gods. Still, let it be granted that this whole wrong was Malchus' own and came of his own intent.

What then? When I made my request, did you hear me say, 'Save for us a man who has done no wrong and has everywhere been a sleepless guardian of justice'? But if that had been so, he would have saved himself, having his safety in <the> facts themselves. I said that the man held what belonged to others, and admitted it, and would pay it back, but that because of certain fine deeds he deserved to suffer nothing more. And in saying this I seemed to be saying what was just, and you said you would act no otherwise; and I believed you, and reported the kind news both to the man himself and to our other friends, at which they praised you and rejoiced with Malchus. You could not say that this is not so.

And yet a man who was not going to do what he said he would do ought not even to have said that he would do it. For it was easy to answer: 'My dearest friend, I want this, but Malchus' wickedness prevents the favour, demanding blows and all the rest, both what comes before them and what comes after them.' For there was certainly no fear that in anger I would put the governor in chains, nor that I would become hostile. For no one was so unreasonable as to blame the intention of the man who refused rather than the nature of the case. No, I would have been grateful to him for having heard the truth, and for neither being deceived myself nor deceiving anyone else.

As it is, the shame is great: one thing was reported, another was done; mild things were hoped for, savage things have appeared; and those whose business is to speak ill of me have gained a starting-point for what they want, saying precisely this, that I, not you, was the father of those words, and that by a fabricated expectation I made the evil greater for Malchus, who was looking towards better things but met with worse. And I, an old man, run the risk of earning a name that I did not earn even in a dream when I was young.

24. 'And yet', he says, 'Malchus found me gentle on the first day.' What of it? I myself was not asking for one day, and your promises covered the whole. For what advantage is there in a milder day before the brutal one that was to come after it, the one sparing, the other destroying? Nor would a doctor, if he killed tomorrow the man he saved today, have a right to recall his fee for today's work, or would he escape hatred because of the second. Nor again does a brigand who first feasts the man he has caught and then butchers him butcher him any less because of the meal that went before. And we know that the Dioscuri escort those to whom they are kindly as far as the harbours, both themselves and their cargo, and do not rescue them from one wave and abandon them to another.

So the pleasure of that day was quenched by the one that followed, while what was done on the second day <needs the help of doctors>. Then, the one was a shadow and nothing, the other truly strong and great.

26. And he even calls me ungrateful, though I have received a great favour: for it was thanks to me that Malchus was not tortured with the most horrible torture, nor had his head cut off. And who taught you this clever thing, if not the man who taught others too, that Libyan, that Irus, then Midas? Whenever he killed someone by the sword, he expected the dead man's family to be grateful to him that the death had not been by fire; and whenever he made the death by fire, he again counted it a favour that the dead man was not deprived of burial.

And you are walking the same road, not seeing those who laugh at you. For who, child or man, is so foolish as not easily to grasp the argument? For when will you not be among those who have done a favour, since there is always something that has been left out? For if you had cut off his head, you would have said what the former man said; and if limb by limb, you would have cited the burial. And if you had given the corpse to dogs and birds, it would be possible to say: 'But I did not throw him into cauldrons, nor boil and eat him.'

But, I think, it is very laughable to call these things a favour. Or if you had gouged out his eyes, would you have expected me to think you had done me a favour by not taking away his tongue as well, just as if someone who had confiscated a man's property were to call it kindness that he had not also voted him into slavery? So far, then, were these things from being a favour that he did not dare to say at the time of my entreaties that he would grant me that the man should not suffer this and that, but nothing else. And yet, if it was a favour, what harm was there in its being made known even before it was given?

29. 'And he provoked me', he says, 'with certain rather bold words. If these had not been said, he would not have suffered these things.' How then, before these words were spoken, did you claim that there were wrongs deserving the utmost punishment? So let him not say both. But if the damage to the emperor's household demanded so great a punishment, why does he mention the words in the courtroom? And if these needed to be punished in this way, let the matter of the money be passed over in silence; he himself says it would not have been examined, by claiming that the words caused his anger.

Let us then consider the words themselves which, as this man says, stung him. He admitted that he owed it and would pay it, but not immediately; he needed two months. Are these things deserving of anger? Of rage? Of harshness? Of savagery? Since the race of men began, and with it collecting debts and owing them, has this not been the help for debtors: they ask for postponement, and those who may refuse grant it, and in this give the debtors breathing space? For what I could not settle today, I could later. The lender holds off, one for two months, another three, another twice as many, another a year, another even longer; and then, later recovering what he advanced, he praises himself and his own delay, as being what actually got the money repaid.

Some indeed have bound a debtor with unbearable constraints and sent him to the noose, and then had no one to go after themselves. And this has been thought so humane that the law has even made the judge master of the time-limit in such cases. And if the debtor meets with no fairness from his creditors, by taking refuge there he obtains a stay of immediate payment, and the creditor can no longer throttle him or lay hands on him.

But you, on hearing 'two months', leapt upon Malchus. Why? Did this undo your belt? Did it rob you of some of your term of office? Did it bring you poverty? Did it make you weaker than those who would like to be your enemies? Did it change the reputation you have with the ruler into its opposite? Did it prevent you from obtaining office? Was it so very dreadful a thing to be allowed to say that two months would collect this gold that holds together the empire of the Romans? No, I think the months were a pretext, and the intent was to strike, in Malchus, those who care for Malchus. These this man has not stopped barking at; but Malchus, having found helpers in many places, was not going to flee and jump across to him.

And let us grant that what he said about the two months was said rather boorishly. Then it would have been enough to throw him out without [his request being] granted, and in that to exact the penalty; but there was no occasion for blows, and such blows and so many, nor on the naked body, nor on a body turned this way and that so that no part was left free of blows. So there was not much justice in what Malchus suffered; but even if one were to grant it, I myself could still complain that even so I have been insulted.

34. 'But I have come,' says Antiochus, 'because he sent me, and this is a sign of one who is removing the grievance.' Rather, this is a sign of one who admits the grievance; but what removes it no one could show me. For what has been done is beyond remedy, and until Severus is shown not to have said what he said, it is impossible that I have not been wronged.

Now if we allow wrongdoers, after doing what they please, to have as friends those who have suffered at their hands, at the cost of a few syllables, we would be giving them a great advantage, if, while they behave outrageously towards whomever they wish, they are not even hated by those they have insulted, as if they had themselves condemned what they did. And it will be easy, I think, for the man who has spoken abuse, and the one who has struck, and the one who has done harm, and those who dare greater things, by coming forward in the humility of the penitent, to have as friends those who would have grounds to accuse them.

But somehow I have been carried off into the case of those who admit their fault. For our man nowhere utters this, nor did Antiochus say anywhere that he brought this word, nor did any of us hear it. Why then should anyone pardon a man who says that he has done no wrong either to me or to that man, but that he has done just what a god would?

37. 'But if not in words, then in deeds he has admitted it, being in distress and longing for your company. And you, having convicted many of wronging you, were reconciled.' Certainly. But there are also some with whom I have not been reconciled, nor does time stand still to see this, not even the time among the gods below; but soul will shun souls and not converse, as in the case of Ajax of Salamis, when Odysseus in Hades found fault with his own victory.

I know where hatred should be ended, and I know in what cases never. And I could tell of a man with whom I made a truce. What persuaded me of this? That nothing irreparable had been done to those under his hand about whom I had petitioned. Someone asked for a number of days to visit some of his own estates. The governor did not grant it. I went away indignant. Time put my anger to sleep; for the man about whom I had spoken had suffered not ill, but only not good. For another I asked that a sentence be quashed, as the law allowed, but he refused. And this caused an enmity up to a point, but not a complete one. Afterwards I went back where I used to. For nothing shameful had happened to my friend, nor was he dishonoured in what he had staked.

But the present affair, what was done by this man and to this man, needs the spirit of Aeschylus and Sophocles; it calls for the enmity to be endless. And the things that have moved so great a city to lamentation will thrust me back from his doors, all but crying out: 'Do not, do not lay aside the enmity, do not quench the hatred, do not court a snake, do not be base towards a suppliant who has become, by what he suffered, a slave of his own slaves, unable to reproach his household servants, unable to accuse his sons of idleness, unable to blame his wife for sleeping, stripped everywhere of his pride, and cast out of his freedom of speech by the rods and what came along with them.'

40. Antiochus spoke too of office and power, and how great it is, and how enmity with a governor is not without danger. I have long known this, but I have never betrayed justice for fear of power, nor have I flattered such men rather than stand with the wronged. Of this a long time is my witness, and many cities, many provinces, many people, many places, and, greatest of all, the gods, who have been to me in place of arms and ramparts and walls. For I would not say that I was not plotted against, but that I was kept safe by the favour of the gods, as was that man who took Troy, by the goodwill of Athena, who helped him in all else and also set his house in order.

I have persuaded myself, then, that I shall find them no less zealous allies, and that they will not condemn their care for me and abandon me to a governor's power, nor betray in old age one whom in youth they thought worthy of their providence. And with the help of the gods a man once trusted that, even with a single companion, he would put such an end as he wished to the Trojan War.

In short, if we obey in this out of fear, what of all things shall we not grant out of fear, so that our safety would lie in his asking nothing improper? Come, if he bade me go to the schoolroom after bathing and drinking, shall I obey? What, to hate one of my friends, shall I obey? What, to hold dice in my hands instead of books, shall I obey? And indeed, if we put up with this now because of the power he has, [we shall put up with] each of those too [for the same reason]. For while the same fear lies upon us, there is no escaping anything.

43. 'But many,' he says, 'will be deprived of help, unless you go in to him and help them.' And what is there to persuade me that by doing this I shall relieve anyone's misfortune? What has been done does not say so, and, according to Isocrates, one judges the unseen from the seen. If there are some who have been well treated by him on my account, one should believe something similar will happen; but if no one is ignorant of what happened to Malchus, it is foolish to deceive ourselves and be lured by what will never be.

Apart from this, I see no shortage of allies who will stand by those in need. Instead of waiting for petitions, they themselves hunt for ways to drag in those in need. And there are many all over the city who are not at all ashamed to do this for pay. So let no one fear this. The fact that countless men have held office has made many able to give aid. Those men will both do good and receive good in return, dearest Antiochus, who have enslaved the fellow by the praises of his wicked deeds at drinking parties. For as though they were lunching with Aeacus and not with a hanger-on of the marketplace, without examining the nature of what he does, they take it as proof that justice is in those deeds that he is the one who did them. So, being among cups that bear such flowers, he becomes quick to grant favours.

45. Stand up, then, and report this. 'On what feet shall I return?' you will perhaps say. On those of Ajax, on those of Odysseus. For the failure to persuade was not theirs, but belonged to the man who had committed such outrages, which I think will be the view now too. But am I to go to him, and see him, and keep company with him, and sit near him, and converse as friends do, knowing what words will follow such deeds? For what will men say? What women? What children? What youth? What old age? 'This is the compassionate one? This the merciful one? This the enemy of the harsh? This the friend of the gentle?' Do we think this will please the sun? Or the day? Or the night? Or the spirits of each? Or Justice who sees all things? 'Then he praises living freely, yet is not ashamed to act like those who are willing slaves? For he did not go in to fight him and to expose all the wrongs he had done; no, this is wholly the act of one who cowered, was afraid, and knows how to flatter.'

Do you want these things, dear Antiochus, said about your friend? These darts to come at me? And how do you think the other governors will be towards me, having such examples to look to? Will they not say such things among themselves: 'This man, when dishonoured, knows not how great a governor is; when honoured, he hisses'?

47. 'For he will leap up,' he says, 'if you appear, and kiss your head.' Certainly. So he has countless others. And I know only very few who have not received this. For he is friend to no one, nor would he wish any human being to prosper; but he deceives with his lips, and would like each man to think he has been preferred by him above the rest. Since he knows he will win no praisers by his deeds themselves, he has invented this art, so that his honours have come to rank as dishonours.

48. 'But I hate wickedness,' he says, 'and [my] nature had to prevail here too, and I heard arguments intended to help Malchus.' But that is not what Mareas says, nor the man who sits as his assessor, through whom everything is for money, everything for sale. And heavy is the snowfall of takings, with the plaintiff paying and the defendant paying, neither knowing what the other does, but both resting on the same hope. Nor is it possible for the losers to recover what they paid out, since the matter has been settled beforehand by certain oaths. Nothing is free: not a vote, not an admission, not a name, not a syllable, not a letter.

And these things are sold so openly, fearing no eye or ear, that there is a belief that they trust in prophecies and so shrink from nothing. At any rate, as men who will pay no penalty they reap everything, while all the Syrians cry out that, of all who have grown rich from these very seats [of office], all are paupers compared with this man. Naturally, then, they also buy the governors in higher posts, and those at whose hands they would have died, if anything just were done, these they hold under their control. So, while this man was away, the other one ate; when he came, both did. Or what else could ever have stopped those thunders and those lightnings? Nothing.

But this Mareas has a relative by marriage more powerful than any Medea. And the deed was his, but, hiding the truth, they made out Victor to be the reconciler in the eyes of many onlookers. He released a man who was no longer even in chains, and the hater of wickedness sent Mareas off again to reap the same crops, to gather the same vintage, to shear the same flocks; he sent him again to the same springs and the same fountains of gold and silver. These he collected little by little and brought to a great size. For the man who sends him to the same fodder knows that the feast belongs to both, to the one sent and to the one who sent him.

And what wonder is it if this man yields to gains so great? He even cheated the receivers in the valuation of what the emperor gives to officials out of the revenues coming to him from the land, forcing them to buy things they had no need of, and in addition wronging them with measures that did not accord with the law. So he sold, and they bought at a loss, and poverty was compelled to create wealth. Yet even so, if you do not call him an Aristides, you will be doing him wrong.

52. O Fortune, who does whatever she wishes, and does not consider whether she wishes rightly or not, but makes displays of her power in not preserving what is fitting! She gave Sicily to Dionysius, who knew the donkeys of his father which he used to drive; she gave the same island to Agathocles, and his father the potter did not hinder it. And why should I mention Hermias, the eunuch and tyrant of Atarneus? Did not Porus, the son of a barber, rule the Indians? Shall I speak of Bardylis the charcoal-burner, to whom the Illyrians did obeisance? After these, Orthagoras the cook ruling Sicyon would seem a small matter.

And now too, then, we see that the goddess is the same. And this kind of display has not ceased, but men unknown even to their neighbours, who would rightly be herding goats or tending sheep or cattle or be among the swineherds, are borne aloft on the wings given by Fortune. She is ill spoken of everywhere for not reserving these things for virtues alone, but she will do, as long as there is a human race, what she has so often done. Even if you see a swineherd following his pigs, do not spit on him in contempt, reflecting that perhaps this man too may be adorned by Fortune.

54. This in itself is dreadful and in no way bearable, that some are brought from the mills and the sleepless nights in them to power and the splendours of office; but it becomes much more dreadful and more unbearable when those transferred from such things to such positions refuse to know who they are and from whom they are sprung, and do not allow their former state any room in their soul, but drive it out and make the whole of it belong to the later.
Such is this man of ours. He ought to be fighting innkeepers over dung by the Tigris, but he has become master of throwing a large part of the world into turmoil.
But, O gods and goddesses, persuade Fortune <to do> what is fitting regarding Severus, and casting him out of the irrational favour she has shown him, show him to be the jackdaw in the fable.
